(p-1296) When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the state of the people of the Fire, that the word of punishment had come due against them, and that they are the companions of the Fire, He then mentioned their condition after entering the Fire, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve will be called out to﴾.

Al-Wahidi said: The commentators said: When they see their deeds, look into their record, are cast into the Fire, and loathe themselves for the evil of their conduct, a caller will call out to them when they witness the punishment of God: "The aversion of God toward you in the world, when you were summoned to faith and you disbelieved, ﴿is greater than your aversion toward yourselves﴾ today."

Al-Akhfash said: This lam in "la-maqtu" (the emphatic lam) is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida', the emphatic lam), placed after "yunadawna" (they are called), because its meaning is "it is said to them," and calling out is a form of speech.

Al-Kalbi said: Each person among the people of the Fire will say to himself: "I loathe you, O self!" Then the angels will say to them, while they are in the Fire: "The aversion of God toward you in the world is greater than your aversion toward yourselves today."

Al-Hasan said: They will be given their record, and when they look at their evil deeds they will loathe themselves, and then they will be called out: "The aversion of God toward you in the world ﴿when you were summoned to faith﴾ is greater than your aversion toward yourselves, when you witnessed the Fire." The adverbial phrase "idh tud'awna" (when you were summoned) is in the accusative, governed by an omitted implied element that is indicated by what is mentioned, i.e., "your aversion at the time of your being summoned." It was also said that it is governed by an omitted element, namely "remember" (udhkuru), and it was also said that it is governed by the aversion mentioned. Maqt (aversion) is the strongest hatred.

Then He, glory be to Him, informed us of what they say in the Fire, saying: ﴿They will say: "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice."﴾ The word "ithnatayn" (two) in both places is an adjective for an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: "You made us die two deaths, and You gave us life two lives." The meaning of the two deaths is that they were drops of semen with no life in the loins of their fathers, then He made them die after they had become living in the world. The meaning of the two lives is that He gave them the first life in the world, then gave them life again at the Resurrection. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die, then He will give you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: they were made to die in the world when their terms ended, then God gave them life in their graves for questioning, then they were made to die again, then God gave them life in the Hereafter. The reasoning behind this view is that death is the removal of life, and a drop of semen has no life.

The reasoning behind the first view is that death may be applied to one who lacks life from the outset, and the majority of the early scholars (al-salaf) adopted the first interpretation.

Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of the verse is that He created them in the loins of Adam, brought them out, gave them life, took their covenant, then made them die, then gave them life in the world, then made them die.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned their confession, after they had become inhabitants of the Fire, of what they had denied in the world, saying, relating about them: ﴿So we confess our sins﴾ that we committed in the world, namely denying the messengers, associating others with God, and abandoning His monotheism. They confessed at a time when confession would not benefit them, and they repented at a time when repentance would not benefit them. They made this confession a preface to their saying: ﴿Is there any way to get out?﴾, meaning: is there any way for us to leave the Fire and return to the world? A similar statement is their saying which God related about them: ﴿Is there any way to get out?﴾ [al-Shura: 44], and His saying: ﴿Return us, so that we may act righteously﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12], and His saying: ﴿If only we could be returned﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and so on.

Then God, glory be to Him, responded to their saying with His words: ﴿That is because when God alone was called upon, you disbelieved﴾, meaning: that which you are in, of punishment, is because, when God alone was called upon in the world, to the exclusion of others, you disbelieved in Him and abandoned His monotheism; and if others were associated with Him, such as idols or other things, you believed in that association and answered the one who called to it. Thus He, glory be to Him, explained to them the cause that prevented them from responding to leave the Fire, which is what they were engaged in: abandoning the monotheism of God and associating others with Him in worship, the foremost form of which is supplication. The position of ﴿dhalikum﴾ (that) is nominative, as it is either a predicate with an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is that," or a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "that is the punishment you are in, because of that cause." There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "So they were answered that there is no way to return," because when God alone was called upon, the judgment belongs to God alone, to the exclusion of others. He is the One who decreed for you eternal abiding in the Fire and no leaving from it; the Exalted, who is far above having any like in His essence or His attributes; and the Great, who is too great to have any equal, consort, child, or partner.

﴿He is the One who shows you His signs﴾, meaning: the proofs of His oneness and the indications of His power. ﴿And sends down provision for you from the sky﴾, meaning: rain, for it is the cause of sustenance.

He, glory be to Him, combined the showing of signs and the sending down of provision, because the manifestation of signs sustains religions, and provision sustains bodies. These signs are the created signs that God, glory be to Him, placed in His heavens, His earth, and what is in them and between them.

The majority of readers read "yunazzilu" with the doubled letter (intensive form). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the single letter.

﴿And none will be mindful except those who turn back﴾, meaning: none is mindful or admonished by those dazzling signs, so that they use them as evidence for monotheism and the truth of the promise and the threat, except those who turn back, that is, those who return to obedience to God through what they gain from contemplating the signs of God.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned the proofs He established for monotheism, He commanded His servants to call upon Him and to devote religion to Him, saying: ﴿So call upon God, devoting religion sincerely to Him﴾, meaning: if the matter is as has been mentioned, then call upon God alone, devoting worship sincerely to Him, which He commanded you to perform, even if the disbelievers dislike that. Do not turn to their dislike, and leave them to die of their rage and perish from their regret.

"Rafi' al-darajat" (Exalted in ranks): the raising of "Rafi' al-darajat" is because it is another predicate of the preceding subject, meaning: He is the One who shows you His signs, and He is Exalted in ranks; likewise "Dhu al-'arsh" (Lord of the Throne) is a third predicate. It is also permissible for "Rafi' al-darajat" to be a subject whose predicate is "Dhu al-'arsh," and it is permissible for both to be predicates of an omitted subject. "Rafi'" is an intensive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah).

The meaning is: Exalted in attributes, or Exalted in the ranks of His angels, meaning their ascending stages, or Exalted in the ranks of His prophets and His friends in Paradise.

Al-Kalbi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Exalted above the seven heavens. In this sense "Rafi'" means "raising" (rafi' as active participle). The meaning of "Dhu al-'arsh" is its owner, its creator, and the one who manages it. This implies the loftiness of His rank and the greatness of His dominion, and whoever is like this is the one who has the right to be worshipped and to whom sincerity is owed.

The clause ﴿He casts the Spirit by His command﴾ is in the nominative position, as another predicate for the preceding subject or the omitted one. Its meaning is that He, glory be to Him, casts the revelation ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. Revelation is called "spirit" because people come to life through it from the death of disbelief, just as bodies live by spirits. The phrase "min amrihi" (by His command) is connected to "yulqi" (casts), and "min" here indicates the starting point (min li-ibtida' al-ghayah). It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted element as a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) for "al-Rūḥ" (the Spirit). A similar verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit by Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. It was also said that "al-Rūḥ" is Gabriel, as in His saying: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193–194], and His saying: ﴿The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord in truth﴾ [al-Nahl: 102]. ﴿Upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ refers to the prophets. The meaning of "min amrihi" (by His command) is "from His decree."

﴿So that he may warn of the Day of Meeting﴾. The majority read "li-yundhira" as active, with the accusative on "al-yawm" (the day), and the agent is God, glory be to Him, or the Messenger, or whomever He wills. The object of the warning is omitted, and its implied form is: "so that he may warn of the punishment on the Day of Meeting." Ubayy and a group read it the same way except that they put "al-yawm" in the nominative as the agent, metaphorically.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read "li-tundhira" with the feminine prefix, so that the agent is the second-person pronoun referring to the Messenger, or a pronoun referring back to the Spirit, since it is permissible to feminize it.

Al-Yamani read "li-yundhara" in the passive, with "yawm" in the nominative as a substitute for the agent.

The meaning of "Day of Meeting" is the day when the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth meet at the place of gathering. Qatadah said this.

Abu al-'Aliyah and Muqatil said: the day when those who worshipped and those who were worshipped meet. It was also said: the oppressor and the oppressed. It was also said: the first and the last. It was also said: the recompense for deeds and the doers.

His saying: ﴿The Day they will emerge﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day of Meeting﴾.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is in the accusative governed by His saying: ﴿nothing about them is hidden from God﴾. It was also said: it is in the accusative governed by an implied "remember." The first is preferable. The meaning of "bariz\u016bn" (emerging) is: coming out of their graves, with nothing concealing them. The clause ﴿nothing about them is hidden from God﴾ is a new sentence explaining their emerging. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "bariz\u016bn." It is also permissible for it to be a second predicate for the subject, meaning: nothing about them, nor any of their deeds that they did in the world, is hidden from Him, glory be to Him.

The clause ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾ is a new sentence answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What will be said at the emergence of creatures on that day?" So it is said: "To whom belongs the dominion today?" The commentators said: When all who are in the heavens and the earth have perished, the Lord, blessed and exalted, will say: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. No one answers Him, so He, exalted, answers Himself, saying: ﴿To God, the One, the Subduer﴾. Al-Hasan said: He is the Questioner, exalted, and He is the Answerer when no one else can answer Him, so He answers Himself. It was also said that He commands a herald to call out with this, and the people of the gathering, believers and disbelievers alike, will say: ﴿To God, the One, the Subduer﴾. It was also said that the people of Paradise alone answer the herald with this answer, not the people of the Fire. It was also said that it is a report of what the tongue of the state speaks on that day, due to the cessation of the claims of the falsifiers, as in His saying, exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? Then what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? The Day when no soul will have power for another soul at all, and the command that Day belongs to God﴾ [al-Infitar: 17–19].

His saying: ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned. There is no injustice today. Indeed God is swift in reckoning﴾ is part of the answer according to the view that the one who answers is God, glory be to Him. As for the view that those who answer are all the servants or some of them, it is a new sentence explaining what God, glory be to Him, says after their answer, meaning: today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned of good and evil. There is no injustice today against anyone among them, by a reduction in their reward or an increase in their punishment. Indeed God is swift in reckoning, meaning: His reckoning is swift, because He, glory be to Him, does not need to deliberate about it as others do, given the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything; nothing escapes Him, not even the weight of an atom.

Then God, glory be to Him, commanded His Messenger to warn His servants, saying: ﴿And warn them of the Approaching Day﴾, meaning: the Day of Resurrection, named so because of its nearness. It is said: "Azifa fulan" meaning "so-and-so drew near," yaʾzafu azafan. From this is the saying of al-Nabigha:

"The time of departure has drawn near, though our mounts have not yet moved from our mounts, and it is as if it has already happened."

From this is His saying, exalted: ﴿The Approaching One has drawn near﴾ [al-Najm: 57], meaning the Hour has drawn near. It was also said that the Day of the Approaching is the day of the presence of death, but the first is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: It was called "the Approaching" because it is near, even if people consider its occurrence far off, and whatever is to come is near: ﴿when hearts are at the throats, choking with grief﴾. That is because hearts leave their places out of fear until they reach the throat, as in His saying: ﴿and the hearts reached the throats﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]. "Kazimin" (choking) means grieving, distressed, afflicted, filled with sorrow.

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: when people's hearts are at their throats while they suppress (their grief). Qatadah said: their hearts have risen to their throats from fear, so they neither leave nor return to their places. It was also said: this is an report about the extreme of anguish. He said "kadhimin" (suppressing) with regard to the people, since the meaning is: when the hearts of people are at their throats, so it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause referring to the hearts, and the circumstantial form was pluralized as for rational beings, because what is ascribed to rational beings is ascribed to the hearts, so it was made plural in the same way.

Then He, glorified is He, explained that no one will benefit the disbelievers on that Day, saying: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend﴾, meaning no relative who would benefit them, ﴿nor any intercessor who is obeyed﴾ in his intercession for them. The position of yuṭā' (is obeyed) is in the genitive case (jarr), as it is an attribute (ṣifah) of shafī' (intercessor).

Then He, glorified is He, described the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything, even if it is in the utmost concealment, saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾, which is the furtive glance at what it is not lawful to look at. The sentence is another predicate (khabar) for His saying: "He is the One who shows you". Al-Mu'arrij said: there is inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr) in it, meaning: He knows the treacherous eyes.

Qatadah said: "the treachery of the eyes" is pointing with the eye at what Allah does not love. al-Dahhak said: it is a person's saying "I did not see" when he has seen, and "I saw" when he did not see. Sufyan said: it is the glance after a glance. The first (view) is preferable, and Mujahid said likewise.

﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾ of inner thoughts and what they hide of the disobedience of Allah.

﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, so He recompenses each person with what he deserves of good and evil.

﴿And those you call upon besides Him﴾, meaning those you worship besides Allah, ﴿do not judge anything﴾, because they do not know anything and have no power over anything.

The majority of readers recited "yadʿūna" (they call upon) with the letter yā' (third person), meaning the wrongdoers. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Ḥātim preferred this reading. Nafi', Shaybah and Hisham recited it with the letter tā' (second person), addressing them directly. ﴿Indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, so nothing hidden from what is heard and what is seen escapes Him.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, and al-Ḥakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: ﴿You caused us to die twice and You gave us life twice﴾. He said: it is like the one in al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. They were dead in the loins of their fathers, then He brought them out and gave them life, then He caused them to die, then He will give them life after death.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: you were dust before He created you, so this is one death; then He gave you life and created you, so this is life; then He will cause you to die, and you will return to the graves, so this is another death; then He will resurrect you on the Day of Resurrection, so this is life. Thus they are two deaths and two lives, like His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life﴾, the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿the Day of Meeting﴾, he said: the Day of Resurrection, on which Adam and the last of his offspring will meet. He also narrated from him, saying: the Day of Meeting is the Day of the Imminent (al-Āzifah). Similar to this are the names of the Day of Resurrection, which Allah has magnified and warned His servants about.

'Abd Allah ibn Aḥmad in Zawā'id al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥakim, who authenticated it, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Ḥilyah narrated from him as well, he said: a caller will call out before the Hour: "O people, the Hour has come upon you," and the living and the dead will hear it. Allah will descend to the lowest heaven and say: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer﴾.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in al-Ba'th and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of this.

'Abd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Allah will gather the creation on the Day of Resurrection in one plain, on a white land like a silver ingot, in which Allah has never been disobeyed. The first thing that will be said is a caller calling out: ﴿Whose is the dominion today? It is Allah's, the One, the Subduer﴾, ﴿Today every soul will be recompensed for what it earned; there is no injustice today; indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾. The first of the disputes with which the matter begins will be blood."

Sa'id ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Ḥatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾, he said: a man may be among a group when a woman passes by them, and he shows them that he lowers his gaze from her; but when they are heedless he glances at her, and when they look he lowers his gaze from her. Yet Allah knows from his heart that he wishes to look at her private parts.

Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ṭabarani in al-Awsaṭ, Abu Nu'aym in al-Ḥilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from him concerning the verse, he said: when he looks at her, does he intend treachery or not? ﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾: when he is able to her, will he commit adultery with her or not? Shall I not tell you about the one that follows: ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, He is able to recompense good with good and evil with evil.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Sa'd, who said: "When the Day of the Conquest of Makkah came, the Prophet (ﷺ) granted safety to the people except four men and two women, and he said: 'Kill them even if you find them clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah.' Among them was 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh, who hid with 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him). When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people to the pledge of allegiance, he brought him, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, accept the pledge of 'Abd Allah.' He raised his head and looked at him three times, each time refusing his pledge. Then he turned to his companions and said: 'Was there not among you a rightly guided man who would stand up to this one when he saw me withholding my hand from his pledge, and kill him?' They said: 'How would we know, O Messenger of Allah, what is in your mind? Why did you not signal to us with your eye?' He said: 'It is not befitting for a Prophet to have the treachery of the eyes.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 40, verses 21–39:

When Allah, glorified is He, warned them with the conditions of the Hereafter, He followed this with an explanation of warning them with the conditions of this world. So He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ He, glorified is He, guided them to take a lesson from others, since those who disbelieved and passed away from among the disbelievers ﴿were greater than them in strength﴾, than these present disbelievers, and more powerful, ﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾, by what they built on it of fortresses and palaces, and by what they had of numbers and equipment. When they denied their messengers, Allah destroyed them. His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (fa-yanzurū, "and see") is either jussive by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ (yasīrū), or subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. His saying ﴿كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً﴾ ("they were stronger than them in power") explains the disparity between the condition of these and those, and His saying "وآثارًا" ("and traces") is coordinated upon "قُوَّةً" ("power").

The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and the ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ in the nominative, as the agent.

﴿And Musa said: "Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."﴾ Abu Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿عُذْتُ﴾ (ʿudhtu) with idghām (assimilation) of the dhāl, while the rest read it with izhār (clear pronunciation). When Fir'awn threatened him with killing, he sought refuge in Allah, mighty and majestic is He, from every one who magnifies himself against belief in Allah, who does not believe in the resurrection and the gathering. Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said﴾: Al-Hasan, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: he was a Copt and a paternal cousin of Fir'awn, and he was the one who was saved along with Musa, and he is the one meant by His saying ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). It was said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, but this contradicts what is in the verse. It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and the ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ in the nominative, as the agent.

The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. When Fir'awn threatened him with killing, he sought refuge in Allah, mighty and majestic is He, from every one who magnifies himself against belief in Allah, who does not believe in the resurrection and the gathering. Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said﴾: Al-Hasan, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: he was a Copt and a paternal cousin of Fir'awn, and he was the one who was saved along with Musa, and he is the one meant by His saying ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). It was said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, but this contradicts what is in the verse. It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The first: if he were excessive and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor strengthened him with miracles. The second: if he were like that, Allah would forsake him and destroy him, so you have no need to kill him. The excessive one (musrif) is the one who persists in sins and multiplies them, and the liar (kadhdhab) is the one who fabricates.

﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, prevailing in the land﴾. The believing man reminded them of the kingdom they were in, so that they would thank Allah and not persist in their disbelief. The meaning of ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ (ẓāhirīn, "prevailing") is dominance over people, victory over them, and supremacy over them. The land is the land of Egypt, and ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: who will prevent us from His punishment and come between us and it when it arrives? For this reason he said: ﴿I only show you what I see﴾. Ibn Zayd said: that is, I only advise you with what I see for myself. Al-Dahhak said: "I only inform you of what I know." The seeing here is of the heart, not of sight, and the second object is ﴿إلّا ما أرى﴾ (illā mā ara, "except what I see").

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right direction﴾, i.e., by this opinion I only guide you to the path of truth. The majority read ﴿الرَّشادِ﴾ (al-rashād) with the shīn lightened, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with the shīn doubled, as an intensive form like ḍarrāb. Al-Nahhas said: it is a solecism (laḥn), and there is no basis for it.

He said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him with a severe choking. Then Abu Bakr came, seized his two shoulders, pushed him away from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?﴾"

Abu Nuʿaym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah*, and al-Bazzar, transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he said: "O people, inform me: who is the bravest of people?" They said: "You." He said: "As for me, I have not fought anyone except that I got the better of him. But inform me of the bravest of people." They said: "We do not know, so who?" Abu Bakr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh seized him: this one was pushing him, and that one was pulling him, and they were saying: 'You are the one who made the gods into one god.' By Allah, none came close to us except Abu Bakr, striking this one, pushing that one, and pulling this one, while he was saying: 'Woe to you! Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah?'" Then he lifted a cloak that was upon him and wept until his beard was soaked. Then he said: "I ask you by Allah: is the believer of the family of Fir'awn better, or Abu Bakr?" The people were silent. He said: "Will you not answer? By Allah, one hour of Abu Bakr is better than a believer like the believer of the family of Fir'awn. That one was a man who concealed his faith, and this one was a man who announced his faith."

So He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ He, glorified is He, guided them to take a lesson from others, since those who disbelieved and passed away from among the disbelievers ﴿were greater than them in strength﴾, than these present disbelievers, and more powerful, ﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾, by what they built on it of fortresses and palaces, and by what they had of numbers and equipment. When they denied their messengers, Allah destroyed them. His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (fa-yanzurū, "and see") is either jussive by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ (yasīrū), or subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. His saying ﴿كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً﴾ ("they were stronger than them in power") explains the disparity between the condition of these and those, and His saying "وآثارًا" ("and traces") is coordinated upon "قُوَّةً" ("power").

The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and the ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ in the nominative, as the agent.

Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The clause ﴿وقَدْ جاءَكم بِالبَيِّناتِ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ("while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "and the situation is that he has certainly come to you with the evident miracles and the manifest indications of his prophethood and the soundness of his message." Then he gently addressed them in defending him, saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, there will afflict you some of what he promises you﴾. This statement was not from doubt on his part, for he was a believer as Allah described him, and a believer does not doubt. The meaning of ﴿يُصِبْكم بَعْضُ الَّذِي يَعِدُكُمْ﴾ ("some of what he promises you will befall you") is that if not all of it befalls you, then at least some of it will befall you. The nūn of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (yakun, "he is") was deleted in both places for lightness due to frequent use, as Sibawayh said.

Abu Ubaydah and Abu al-Haytham said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ, "some") here means ﴿كُلٍّ﴾ (kull, "all"), that is: "all of what he promises you will befall you." Abu Ubaydah cited as evidence the verse of Labid:

Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

There is nothing in the two verses that proves what they claim. As for the verse of Labid, it has been said that he meant by "some souls" his own soul. There is no necessity that compels one to interpret what is in the verse in this way, because he intended to descend to their level and give them the impression that he does not believe in the validity of his prophethood, as His saying ﴿concealing his faith﴾ indicates. The people of the meanings said: this is on the basis of supporting the argument, as if he said to them: "At the very least, if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you, and in some of that is your destruction." So what is achieved by the part is what is achieved by the whole. Al-Layth said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ) here is superfluous, meaning: "what he promises you will befall you." It was said: this punishment which he speaks of in this world will befall you, and it is some of what he threatens you with of punishment. It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. When Fir'awn threatened him with killing, he sought refuge in Allah, mighty and majestic is He, from every one who magnifies himself against belief in Allah, who does not believe in the resurrection and the gathering. Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said﴾: Al-Hasan, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: he was a Copt and a paternal cousin of Fir'awn, and he was the one who was saved along with Musa, and he is the one meant by His saying ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). It was said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, but this contradicts what is in the verse. It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The first: if he were excessive and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor strengthened him with miracles. The second: if he were like that, Allah would forsake him and destroy him, so you have no need to kill him. The excessive one (musrif) is the one who persists in sins and multiplies them, and the liar (kadhdhab) is the one who fabricates.

﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, prevailing in the land﴾. The believing man reminded them of the kingdom they were in, so that they would thank Allah and not persist in their disbelief. The meaning of ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ (ẓāhirīn, "prevailing") is dominance over people, victory over them, and supremacy over them. The land is the land of Egypt, and ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: who will prevent us from His punishment and come between us and it when it arrives? For this reason he said: ﴿I only show you what I see﴾. Ibn Zayd said: that is, I only advise you with what I see for myself. Al-Dahhak said: "I only inform you of what I know." The seeing here is of the heart, not of sight, and the second object is ﴿إلّا ما أرى﴾ (illā mā ara, "except what I see").

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right direction﴾, i.e., by this opinion I only guide you to the path of truth. The majority read ﴿الرَّشادِ﴾ (al-rashād) with the shīn lightened, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with the shīn doubled, as an intensive form like ḍarrāb. Al-Nahhas said: it is a solecism (laḥn), and there is no basis for it.

He said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him with a severe choking. Then Abu Bakr came, seized his two shoulders, pushed him away from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?﴾"

Abu Nuʿaym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah*, and al-Bazzar, transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he said: "O people, inform me: who is the bravest of people?" They said: "You." He said: "As for me, I have not fought anyone except that I got the better of him. But inform me of the bravest of people." They said: "We do not know, so who?" Abu Bakr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh seized him: this one was pushing him, and that one was pulling him, and they were saying: 'You are the one who made the gods into one god.' By Allah, none came close to us except Abu Bakr, striking this one, pushing that one, and pulling this one, while he was saying: 'Woe to you! Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah?'" Then he lifted a cloak that was upon him and wept until his beard was soaked. Then he said: "I ask you by Allah: is the believer of the family of Fir'awn better, or Abu Bakr?" The people were silent. He said: "Will you not answer? By Allah, one hour of Abu Bakr is better than a believer like the believer of the family of Fir'awn. That one was a man who concealed his faith, and this one was a man who announced his faith."

So He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ He, glorified is He, guided them to take a lesson from others, since those who disbelieved and passed away from among the disbelievers ﴿were greater than them in strength﴾, than these present disbelievers, and more powerful, ﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾, by what they built on it of fortresses and palaces, and by what they had of numbers and equipment. When they denied their messengers, Allah destroyed them. His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (fa-yanzurū, "and see") is either jussive by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ (yasīrū), or subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. His saying ﴿كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً﴾ ("they were stronger than them in power") explains the disparity between the condition of these and those, and His saying "وآثارًا" ("and traces") is coordinated upon "قُوَّةً" ("power").

The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and the ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ in the nominative, as the agent.

Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The clause ﴿وقَدْ جاءَكم بِالبَيِّناتِ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ("while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "and the situation is that he has certainly come to you with the evident miracles and the manifest indications of his prophethood and the soundness of his message." Then he gently addressed them in defending him, saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, there will afflict you some of what he promises you﴾. This statement was not from doubt on his part, for he was a believer as Allah described him, and a believer does not doubt. The meaning of ﴿يُصِبْكم بَعْضُ الَّذِي يَعِدُكُمْ﴾ ("some of what he promises you will befall you") is that if not all of it befalls you, then at least some of it will befall you. The nūn of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (yakun, "he is") was deleted in both places for lightness due to frequent use, as Sibawayh said.

Abu Ubaydah and Abu al-Haytham said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ, "some") here means ﴿كُلٍّ﴾ (kull, "all"), that is: "all of what he promises you will befall you." Abu Ubaydah cited as evidence the verse of Labid:

Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

There is nothing in the two verses that proves what they claim. As for the verse of Labid, it has been said that he meant by "some souls" his own soul. There is no necessity that compels one to interpret what is in the verse in this way, because he intended to descend to their level and give them the impression that he does not believe in the validity of his prophethood, as His saying ﴿concealing his faith﴾ indicates. The people of the meanings said: this is on the basis of supporting the argument, as if he said to them: "At the very least, if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you, and in some of that is your destruction." So what is achieved by the part is what is achieved by the whole. Al-Layth said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ) here is superfluous, meaning: "what he promises you will befall you." It was said: this punishment which he speaks of in this world will befall you, and it is some of what he threatens you with of punishment. It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. When Fir'awn threatened him with killing, he sought refuge in Allah, mighty and majestic is He, from every one who magnifies himself against belief in Allah, who does not believe in the resurrection and the gathering. Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said﴾: Al-Hasan, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: he was a Copt and a paternal cousin of Fir'awn, and he was the one who was saved along with Musa, and he is the one meant by His saying ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). It was said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, but this contradicts what is in the verse. It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The first: if he were excessive and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor strengthened him with miracles. The second: if he were like that, Allah would forsake him and destroy him, so you have no need to kill him. The excessive one (musrif) is the one who persists in sins and multiplies them, and the liar (kadhdhab) is the one who fabricates.

﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, prevailing in the land﴾. The believing man reminded them of the kingdom they were in, so that they would thank Allah and not persist in their disbelief. The meaning of ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ (ẓāhirīn, "prevailing") is dominance over people, victory over them, and supremacy over them. The land is the land of Egypt, and ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: who will prevent us from His punishment and come between us and it when it arrives? For this reason he said: ﴿I only show you what I see﴾. Ibn Zayd said: that is, I only advise you with what I see for myself. Al-Dahhak said: "I only inform you of what I know." The seeing here is of the heart, not of sight, and the second object is ﴿إلّا ما أرى﴾ (illā mā ara, "except what I see").

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right direction﴾, i.e., by this opinion I only guide you to the path of truth. The majority read ﴿الرَّشادِ﴾ (al-rashād) with the shīn lightened, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with the shīn doubled, as an intensive form like ḍarrāb. Al-Nahhas said: it is a solecism (laḥn), and there is no basis for it.

He said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him with a severe choking. Then Abu Bakr came, seized his two shoulders, pushed him away from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?﴾"

Abu Nuʿaym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah*, and al-Bazzar, transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he said: "O people, inform me: who is the bravest of people?" They said: "You." He said: "As for me, I have not fought anyone except that I got the better of him. But inform me of the bravest of people." They said: "We do not know, so who?" Abu Bakr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh seized him: this one was pushing him, and that one was pulling him, and they were saying: 'You are the one who made the gods into one god.' By Allah, none came close to us except Abu Bakr, striking this one, pushing that one, and pulling this one, while he was saying: 'Woe to you! Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah?'" Then he lifted a cloak that was upon him and wept until his beard was soaked. Then he said: "I ask you by Allah: is the believer of the family of Fir'awn better, or Abu Bakr?" The people were silent. He said: "Will you not answer? By Allah, one hour of Abu Bakr is better than a believer like the believer of the family of Fir'awn. That one was a man who concealed his faith, and this one was a man who announced his faith."

So He said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ He, glorified is He, guided them to take a lesson from others, since those who disbelieved and passed away from among the disbelievers ﴿were greater than them in strength﴾, than these present disbelievers, and more powerful, ﴿and in traces upon the earth﴾, by what they built on it of fortresses and palaces, and by what they had of numbers and equipment. When they denied their messengers, Allah destroyed them. His saying ﴿فَيَنْظُرُوا﴾ (fa-yanzurū, "and see") is either jussive by coordination with ﴿يَسِيرُوا﴾ (yasīrū), or subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. His saying ﴿كانُوا أشَدَّ مِنهم قُوَّةً﴾ ("they were stronger than them in power") explains the disparity between the condition of these and those, and His saying "وآثارًا" ("and traces") is coordinated upon "قُوَّةً" ("power").

The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. The rest read it with a fatha on the yā' and the hā', and the ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ in the nominative, as the agent.
