Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The clause ﴿وقَدْ جاءَكم بِالبَيِّناتِ مِن رَبِّكُمْ﴾ ("while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "and the situation is that he has certainly come to you with the evident miracles and the manifest indications of his prophethood and the soundness of his message." Then he gently addressed them in defending him, saying: ﴿And if he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, there will afflict you some of what he promises you﴾. This statement was not from doubt on his part, for he was a believer as Allah described him, and a believer does not doubt. The meaning of ﴿يُصِبْكم بَعْضُ الَّذِي يَعِدُكُمْ﴾ ("some of what he promises you will befall you") is that if not all of it befalls you, then at least some of it will befall you. The nūn of ﴿يَكُ﴾ (yakun, "he is") was deleted in both places for lightness due to frequent use, as Sibawayh said.

Abu Ubaydah and Abu al-Haytham said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ, "some") here means ﴿كُلٍّ﴾ (kull, "all"), that is: "all of what he promises you will befall you." Abu Ubaydah cited as evidence the verse of Labid:

Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

There is nothing in the two verses that proves what they claim. As for the verse of Labid, it has been said that he meant by "some souls" his own soul. There is no necessity that compels one to interpret what is in the verse in this way, because he intended to descend to their level and give them the impression that he does not believe in the validity of his prophethood, as His saying ﴿concealing his faith﴾ indicates. The people of the meanings said: this is on the basis of supporting the argument, as if he said to them: "At the very least, if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you, and in some of that is your destruction." So what is achieved by the part is what is achieved by the whole. Al-Layth said: ﴿بَعْضُ﴾ (ba'ḍ) here is superfluous, meaning: "what he promises you will befall you." It was said: this punishment which he speaks of in this world will befall you, and it is some of what he threatens you with of punishment. It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿أوْ أنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (aw an yuzhira, "or that he will cause to appear") with ﴿أوْ﴾ (aw, "or"), which is for indefiniteness, and the meaning is that one of the two matters must occur.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. The majority read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنهم﴾ (ashadda minhum, "stronger than them"), while Ibn Amir read ﴿أشَدَّ مِنكم﴾ (ashadda minkum, "stronger than you"), by way of iltifat (a shift in the grammatical person, from third to second). ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins﴾, i.e., because of their sins. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, i.e., no one to repel from them the punishment. The explanation of this verse has already passed in several places.

The reference in His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (dhalika, "that") is to what preceded of seizing them, ﴿because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with evident arguments, ﴿but they disbelieved in what they brought. So Allah seized them. Indeed, He is Strong﴾, who does whatever He wills, nothing can overpower Him, ﴿severe in punishment﴾ for whoever disobeys Him and does not return to Him.

Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take a lesson. He said: ﴿And We had certainly sent Musa with Our signs﴾, which are the nine signs already mentioned in more than one place, ﴿and clear authority﴾, i.e., an evident, manifest proof, which is the Torah.

﴿To Fir'awn and Haman and Qarun, but they said﴾: "He is a sorcerer, a liar," i.e., concerning what he brought. He singled them out for mention because they were the leaders of those who denied Musa: Fir'awn was the king, Haman the minister, and Qarun the owner of wealth and treasures.

﴿So when he came to them with the truth from Us﴾, which are his manifest miracles, ﴿they said: "Kill the sons of those who believe with him and spare their women."﴾ Qatadah said: this killing was other than the first killing, because Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys at the time of Musa's birth, but when Allah sent Musa, he renewed the killing against the Children of Israel. He would order the killing of the males and the leaving alive of the females. A similar statement is Fir'awn's saying ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:127). ﴿And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, i.e., in loss and ruin, because it goes in vain, and what Allah wills befalls them, mighty and majestic is He.

﴿And Fir'awn said: "Leave me to kill Musa."﴾ He said this only because among his close people there were some who would prevent him from killing Musa, fearing that punishment would descend upon them. The meaning is: leave me, let me kill him, and let him call upon his Lord whom he claims sent him to us; let Him prevent him from being killed, if He is able to do so. That is: do not let this frighten you, for he has no real lord; rather, I am your Lord, the Most High. Then he mentioned the reason for which he wished to kill him, saying: ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾ which you are upon, of worshipping other than Allah, and bring you into his religion, which is the worship of Allah alone, ﴿or that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾, i.e., that he will cause dissension and strife among people. The accursed one considered the spread of what Musa called to, and its becoming manifest in the land, and people's guidance by it, to be corruption. Corruption is nothing but what he and those who followed him were upon.

The rest read ﴿وأنْ يُظْهِرَ﴾ (wa-an yuzhira, "and that he will cause to appear") without an alif, with the meaning that both matters occur together. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read ﴿إنِّي أخافُ﴾ (inni akhāf, "indeed I fear") with the yā' vowelled with a fatha. Nafi', Abu Amr and Hafs read ﴿يُظْهِرَ﴾ (yuzhira) with a ḍammah on the yā' and a kasrah on the hā', from ﴿أظْهَرَ﴾ (aẓhara); its subject is the pronoun referring to Musa, and ﴿الفَسادَ﴾ (al-fasād, "corruption") is in the accusative as its direct object. When Fir'awn threatened him with killing, he sought refuge in Allah, mighty and majestic is He, from every one who magnifies himself against belief in Allah, who does not believe in the resurrection and the gathering. Fir'awn enters this generality primarily.

﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn, who concealed his faith, said﴾: Al-Hasan, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: he was a Copt and a paternal cousin of Fir'awn, and he was the one who was saved along with Musa, and he is the one meant by His saying ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said: "O Musa..."﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). It was said that he was from the Children of Israel and not from the family of Fir'awn, but this contradicts what is in the verse. It has been strained to reconcile this by saying that there is an inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir) in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And a believing man from the Children of Israel, who concealed his faith from the family of Fir'awn, said..."

Al-Qushayri said: whoever makes him an Israelite has a far-fetched view, because it is said "kataman-hu amra kadha" (he concealed from him such-and-such a matter), and it is not said "katama minh" (he concealed from him), as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ (An-Nisa' 4:42). The name of this man has been disputed: it was said Habib, and it was said Hizqil, and it was said other than that. Ḥalaḥalat (?) — translated: *"A leaver of places, when I do not like them, or one whose death seizes some souls."*

That is: all souls. This has been objected to, and it was answered that "al-ba'ḍ" is sometimes used in the Arabic language with the meaning of "al-kull," as in the verse of the poet:

*"The patient one may attain some of his need, and with the hasty one there may be error."*

And the saying of another:

*"Indeed, when the affairs are arranged by misfortunes, without the elders, you will see some defect in some of them."*

It was also said: he promised them reward and punishment, so if they disbelieved, the punishment would afflict them, and it is some of what he promised them.

The first: if he were excessive and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor strengthened him with miracles. The second: if he were like that, Allah would forsake him and destroy him, so you have no need to kill him. The excessive one (musrif) is the one who persists in sins and multiplies them, and the liar (kadhdhab) is the one who fabricates.

﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, prevailing in the land﴾. The believing man reminded them of the kingdom they were in, so that they would thank Allah and not persist in their disbelief. The meaning of ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ (ẓāhirīn, "prevailing") is dominance over people, victory over them, and supremacy over them. The land is the land of Egypt, and ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: who will prevent us from His punishment and come between us and it when it arrives? For this reason he said: ﴿I only show you what I see﴾. Ibn Zayd said: that is, I only advise you with what I see for myself. Al-Dahhak said: "I only inform you of what I know." The seeing here is of the heart, not of sight, and the second object is ﴿إلّا ما أرى﴾ (illā mā ara, "except what I see").

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right direction﴾, i.e., by this opinion I only guide you to the path of truth. The majority read ﴿الرَّشادِ﴾ (al-rashād) with the shīn lightened, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with the shīn doubled, as an intensive form like ḍarrāb. Al-Nahhas said: it is a solecism (laḥn), and there is no basis for it.

He said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him with a severe choking. Then Abu Bakr came, seized his two shoulders, pushed him away from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?﴾"

Abu Nuʿaym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah*, and al-Bazzar, transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he said: "O people, inform me: who is the bravest of people?" They said: "You." He said: "As for me, I have not fought anyone except that I got the better of him. But inform me of the bravest of people." They said: "We do not know, so who?" Abu Bakr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh seized him: this one was pushing him, and that one was pulling him, and they were saying: 'You are the one who made the gods into one god.' By Allah, none came close to us except Abu Bakr, striking this one, pushing that one, and pulling this one, while he was saying: 'Woe to you! Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah?'" Then he lifted a cloak that was upon him and wept until his beard was soaked. Then he said: "I ask you by Allah: is the believer of the family of Fir'awn better, or Abu Bakr?" The people were silent. He said: "Will you not answer? By Allah, one hour of Abu Bakr is better than a believer like the believer of the family of Fir'awn. That one was a man who concealed his faith, and this one was a man who announced his faith."

﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is excessive and a liar.﴾ This is part of the speech of the believing man, and it is another argument with two aspects. The first: if he were excessive and a liar, Allah would not have guided him to the clear proofs nor strengthened him with miracles. The second: if he were like that, Allah would forsake him and destroy him, so you have no need to kill him. The excessive one (musrif) is the one who persists in sins and multiplies them, and the liar (kadhdhab) is the one who fabricates.

﴿O my people, for you is the kingdom today, prevailing in the land﴾. The believing man reminded them of the kingdom they were in, so that they would thank Allah and not persist in their disbelief. The meaning of ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ (ẓāhirīn, "prevailing") is dominance over people, victory over them, and supremacy over them. The land is the land of Egypt, and ﴿ظاهِرِينَ﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿So who will support us against the might of Allah if it comes upon us?﴾ That is: who will prevent us from His punishment and come between us and it when it arrives? In this there is a warning from him to them about the vengeance of Allah upon them and the sending down of His punishment on them.

When Fir'awn heard what this man said of sound counsel, he came with a stratagem by which he gave his people the impression that he held a firm place of sincere counsel and care for them, and that he would only take them on a course in which there is the bringing of benefit to them and the averting of harm from them. For this reason he said: ﴿I only show you what I see﴾. Ibn Zayd said: that is, I only advise you with what I see for myself. Al-Dahhak said: "I only inform you of what I know." The seeing here is of the heart, not of sight, and the second object is ﴿إلّا ما أرى﴾ (illā mā ara, "except what I see").

﴿And I only guide you to the path of right direction﴾, i.e., by this opinion I only guide you to the path of truth. The majority read ﴿الرَّشادِ﴾ (al-rashād) with the shīn lightened, while Mu'adh ibn Jabal read it with the shīn doubled, as an intensive form like ḍarrāb. Al-Nahhas said: it is a solecism (laḥn), and there is no basis for it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And a believing man from the family of Fir'awn﴾, that he said: there was no believer in the family of Fir'awn other than him, other than the wife of Fir'awn, and other than the believer who warned Musa, who said: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:20). Ibn al-Mundhir said: I was informed that his name was Hizqil. And ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from Abu Ishaq who said: his name was Habib.

Al-Bukhari and others transmitted through the chain of ʿUrwah, who said: It was said to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs: "Inform us of the most severe thing the polytheists did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was praying in the courtyard of the Ka'bah, ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt came, seized the shoulder of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), twisted his garment around his neck, and choked him with a severe choking. Then Abu Bakr came, seized his two shoulders, pushed him away from the Prophet (ﷺ), and then said: ﴿Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah, while he has certainly come to you with clear proofs from your Lord?﴾"

Abu Nuʿaym in *Fada'il al-Sahabah*, and al-Bazzar, transmitted from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib that he said: "O people, inform me: who is the bravest of people?" They said: "You." He said: "As for me, I have not fought anyone except that I got the better of him. But inform me of the bravest of people." They said: "We do not know, so who?" Abu Bakr said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Quraysh seized him: this one was pushing him, and that one was pulling him, and they were saying: 'You are the one who made the gods into one god.' By Allah, none came close to us except Abu Bakr, striking this one, pushing that one, and pulling this one, while he was saying: 'Woe to you! Will you kill a man because he says: My Lord is Allah?'" Then he lifted a cloak that was upon him and wept until his beard was soaked. Then he said: "I ask you by Allah: is the believer of the family of Fir'awn better, or Abu Bakr?" The people were silent. He said: "Will you not answer? By Allah, one hour of Abu Bakr is better than a believer like the believer of the family of Fir'awn. That one was a man who concealed his faith, and this one was a man who announced his faith."

Then that believing man repeated his admonition to them, and warned them that there would befall them what had befallen those before them. Allah said, relating about him: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions."﴾ That is, like the day of the punishment of the past nations who formed factions against their prophets. He made "day" singular because the plural of "factions" has already sufficed for its plural.

Then he explained "the factions," saying: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Noah, and 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them.﴾ That is, like their condition in punishment, or like their habit of persisting in denial, or like the recompense for what they were upon of disbelief and denial. ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice for the servants.﴾ That is, He does not punish them without sin. The negation of intending injustice necessitates the negation of injustice by the implication of the discourse.

Then he increased in exhortation and reminder, saying: ﴿And O my people, indeed I fear for you the day of calling out.﴾ The majority read "al-tanād" with the dal lightened and the ya' deleted; the original is "al-tanādī," which is the reciprocal form (tafā'ul) from the call (nidā'). It is said: "tanādā al-qawm," meaning some of them called out to one another. Al-Hasan, Ibn al-Sumayfa', Ya'qub, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid read it with the ya' affirmed according to the original. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and 'Ikrimah read it with the dal shaddah. Some people of the language said it is a lahn (solecism), because it is from nadda yandu: when one runs off on his face fleeing. Al-Nahhas said: "This is an error, and the reading is good in the sense of mutual calling."

Al-Dahhak said regarding its meaning: when they hear the roar of Hell, they flee in terror, but they do not reach any region of the earth without finding ranks of angels, so they return to the place where they were. That is His saying: "the day of calling out." According to the reading of the majority, the meaning is: the day when some of them call out to others, or the people of the Fire call out to the people of Paradise and the people of Paradise to the people of the Fire, or on which the happiness of the happy and the wretchedness of the wretched is proclaimed, or the day on which every people is called with their imam. There is no obstacle to carrying it upon all these meanings.

His saying: ﴿The day you turn back fleeing﴾ is a substitute for "the day of calling out": that is, departing from the place of standing toward the Fire, or fleeing from it.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: the meaning is toward the Fire after the reckoning. The clause ﴿You have no protector from Allah against Him﴾ is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, you have no one who protects you from the punishment of Allah and prevents you from it. ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ who guides him to the path of right guidance.

Then he increased in admonishing and reminding them, saying: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾. That is, Joseph son of Jacob; the meaning is that Joseph son of Jacob came to them with miracles and clear signs before the coming of Moses to them, that is, he came to your forefathers, so he made coming to the fathers as coming to the sons.

It was said: what is meant by Joseph here is Joseph son of Ephraim son of Joseph son of Jacob, who had remained among them as a prophet for twenty years.

Al-Naqqash related from al-Dahhak that Allah sent to them a messenger from the jinn called Joseph, but the first is more preferable.

It has been said that Pharaoh of Moses reached the days of Joseph son of Jacob due to his long life. ﴿So you continued in doubt about what he brought you﴾ of the clear proofs and you did not believe in him, until when Joseph perished, ﴿you said: "Allah will never send a messenger after him."﴾ So they disbelieved in him during his life and disbelieved in those after him of the messengers after his death. ﴿Thus Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾. That is: like that clear misguidance, Allah leaves astray whoever is a transgressor in the disobedience of Allah, one who increases in it, a doubter about the religion of Allah, in doubt about His oneness, His promise and His threat.

The relative clause in His saying: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ is a substitute for "whoever," and the plural is in consideration of its meaning; or it is an explanation of it, or an adjective, or in the place of an accusative by the implied "I mean," or the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: they are those who; or a subject whose predicate is "yatba'u" (sets a seal). "Without any authority" is related to "yujadiluna": that is, they dispute concerning the signs of Allah without any clear evidence, and "that came to them" is an adjective of "authority." ﴿It is greatly abhorrent in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believed﴾. It may be intended to express amazement, or to express blame as in "how wretched." The subject of "kabura" is a pronoun referring back to the disputing understood from "yujadiluna." It was said its subject is a pronoun referring back to "man" in "whoever is a transgressor," but the first is more preferable.

His saying "in the sight of Allah" is related to "kabura," and likewise "in the sight of those who believed." It was said: this is from the speech of the believing man. It was said: it is the beginning of speech from Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Thus Allah seals upon every heart of an arrogant tyrant﴾. That is: just as He sealed upon the hearts of these disputers, so likewise He seals, that is, sets a seal upon every heart of an arrogant tyrant.

The majority read "qalb" in the construct with "mutakabbir," and Abu 'Ubayd chose this reading. In the speech there is an omission, and its estimate is: "Thus Allah seals upon every heart of every arrogant one," so the second "kull" is omitted because the first indicates it. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, seals upon the hearts of all arrogant tyrants. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Muhaysin, and Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of the people of Syria read "qalbin" with tanwin, making "mutakabbir" an adjective of it, so "qalb" is meant as the whole person, because the heart is the locus of arrogance and the other limbs follow it in that. Ibn Mas'ud read "'ala qalbi kulli mutakabbir."

Then when Pharaoh heard this, he returned to his arrogance and tyranny, turning away from the admonition, averse to accepting it, and said: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾, that is, a lofty palace, as its explanation has already been mentioned. ﴿That I may reach the means﴾, that is, the ways.

Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and al-Akhfash said: they are the gates. His saying "the means of the heavens" is an explanation of "the means," because when a thing is left vague and then explained, it has more effect on souls. Al-Akhfash, when interpreting the verse, recited the line of Zuhayr:

*"And whoever fears the causes of death, they will reach him, even if he tries the causes of the sky with a ladder."*

It was said: "the means of the heavens" are the matters by which one holds fast. ﴿And I may look upon the God of Moses﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, coordinated with "ablughu" (I may reach), so according to this it falls within the scope of hope.

Al-A'raj, al-Sulami, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Hafs read it in the accusative as an answer to the imperative in his saying "ibni li" (build for me), or as an answer to the hope, as Abu 'Ubayda and others said.

Al-Nahhas said: the meaning of the accusative differs from the meaning of the nominative, because the meaning of the accusative is: when you reach the means, you will look; and the meaning of the nominative is: "perhaps I will reach the means, and perhaps I will look after that." In this is evidence that Pharaoh was in a state of very great ignorance and at a level of very low understanding of the realities of things. ﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾, that is: indeed I think Moses a liar in his claim that he has a god, or in what he claims of messengership. ﴿Thus was made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed﴾, that is: and like that adornment, Satan made attractive to Pharaoh the evil of his deed, of polytheism and denial, so he went on in error, persisted in tyranny, and was turned away from the way, that is, the way of right guidance.

The majority read "wa-ṣudda" with fatha on the ṣad and dal, meaning Pharaoh turned the people away from the way. The Kufans read "wa-ṣuddа" with damma on the ṣad, in the passive voice, and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading; perhaps the reason for choosing it over the other two is that it agrees with what they unanimously agreed on regarding "zuyyina" being in the passive. Yahya ibn Wathhab and 'Alqamah read "ṣidd" with kasra on the ṣad. Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra read with fatha on the ṣad and damma on the dal, with tanwin, as a verbal noun coordinated with "su' 'amalihi," that is: Satan made attractive to him the evil of the deed and the turning away. ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh is nothing but in ruin﴾. "Tabab" means loss and destruction, and from it is ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1].

Then that believing man repeated the reminder and warning, as Allah related about him by His saying: ﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, follow me; I will guide you to the way of right guidance."﴾ That is: follow me in the religion, and I will guide you to the path of right guidance, which is Paradise. It was said: this is from the speech of Moses, but the first is more preferable.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal read "al-Rashshad" with shaddah on the shin, as has been mentioned shortly before in the saying of Pharaoh. It is written in the Mushaf "ittabi'uni" without a ya'. Likewise Abu 'Amr and Nafi' read it with its deletion in pause and its affirmation in continuation. Ya'qub and Ibn Kathir read it with affirmation both in continuation and in pause. The rest read it with deletion both in continuation and in pause. Whoever affirms it follows the original, and whoever deletes it does so because it was deleted in the Mushaf.

﴿O my people, indeed this worldly life is only enjoyment﴾, which one enjoys for days, then it ends and passes away. ﴿And indeed the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾, that is: the settling, because it is everlasting and does not end, and continuous and does not pass away.

﴿Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like﴾. That is: whoever does in the abode of the world any act of disobedience, whatever it may be, will not be recompensed except with its like, and will not be punished except according to its measure. The apparent meaning is that the verse includes everything to which the name "evil deed" applies. It was said it is specific to polytheism, but there is no basis for that. ﴿And whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾, that is: whoever does a righteous deed together with being a believer in Allah and in what His messengers brought, those are the ones who combined righteous deed and faith. ﴿They will enter Paradise, being provided therein without account﴾, that is: without measure and reckoning.

Muqatil said: it means there is no burden upon them regarding what they are given of good in Paradise. It was said: the righteous deed is "there is no god but Allah."

The majority read "yadkhulūna" with a fatha on the ya' (taḥtiyya), in the active voice. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read it with a damma, in the passive voice.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding "mithla da'b," that it means "mithla ḥāl" (like the condition).

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah regarding ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah﴾ that he said: they are the factions: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before with clear proofs﴾ that he said: it is the dream of Joseph; and regarding His saying ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ he said: they are the Jews.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "except in ruin" that he said: loss. 'Abd ibn Humayd related the like of it from Mujahid.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed this worldly life is only enjoyment﴾ that he said: the world is one of the Fridays of the Hereafter, seven thousand years.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the worldly life is enjoyment, and there is nothing of its enjoyment better than a righteous woman, who when you look at her pleases you, and when you are absent from her she guards you in herself and her wealth."

This man of faith repeated his call to them to (follow) God and openly declared his faith. He did not take the earlier approaches, in which he had given them the impression that he was one of them. He stood up to admonish them only out of dislike that some of what Moses had threatened them with should befall them, as a man who loves his people would warn them against falling into what he fears for them. So he said: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter) with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ That is: tell me about your situation. I call you to salvation from the Fire and to entering Paradise through faith in God and obedience to His messengers, while you call me to the Fire by what you want from me of shirk (associating others with God).

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿ma li﴾ (what is with me) is "what is (the matter) with you that I call you," as you say, "What is with me that I see you sad?", meaning "What is with you?"

Then he explained the two calls, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾. So the phrase ﴿tad'unani﴾ (you call me) is either a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿tad'unani﴾ or an explanation of it. ﴿Of which I have no knowledge﴾ means: I have no knowledge that it is a partner of God. ﴿And I call you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving﴾: that is, to the Almighty in His retribution against those who disbelieve, and the Oft-Forgiving toward the sin of those who believe in Him.

﴿Lā jaram﴾ (certainly/undoubtedly): the explanation of this has already been given in Surah Hud. ﴿Jaram﴾ is a past-tense verb with the meaning of ﴿ḥaqqa﴾ (it is true/due). The ﴿lā﴾ that precedes it is for negating what they claimed and refuting what they asserted. The subject of this verb is His saying: ﴿that what you call me to has no call (no efficacy) in this world or in the Hereafter﴾, that is: it is established and necessary that the call to it is void.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it has no answered call that benefits. It has also been said: it has no call that would entitle it to divinity in this world or in the Hereafter.

Al-Kalbi said: it has no intercession. ﴿And that our return is to God﴾: that is, our place of return and our destination is to Him, first through death and then through resurrection, and He will repay each person with what he deserves of good and evil. ﴿And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who greatly increase their disobedience to God. Qatadah and Ibn Sirin said: it means the polytheists. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: they are the foolish, those who shed blood unjustly. Ikrimah said: the tyrants and the arrogant. It has also been said: they are those who transgress the limits of God. The ﴿anna﴾ (that) in both places is coordinated (ʿatf) with the ﴿anna﴾ in His saying ﴿that what you call me to﴾, and the meaning is: and it is true that our return is to God, and it is true that the transgressors, etc.

﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾: when the punishment descends upon you, and you will know that I have indeed exerted myself in advising and admonishing you. In this vagueness there is a threat and intimidation that is not hidden. ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾: that is, I rely upon Him and surrender my affair to Him.

It has been said: he said this when they intended to harm him. Muqatil said: this believing man fled to the mountain and they could not reach him. It has also been said: the speaker is Moses, but the first (view) is preferable.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ (p-1303): that is, God protected him from the evil plot and the harm they intended for him. Qatadah said: God delivered him along with the Children of Israel.

﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh the terrible punishment﴾: that is, it encompassed them and descended upon them, the evil punishment.

Al-Kisa'i said: one says ﴿ḥaqa yaḥīqu ḥayqan wa-ḥuyūqan﴾ (it befell, it encompassed) when it descends and clings. Al-Kalbi said: they drowned in the sea and entered the Fire. By ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ is meant Pharaoh and his people; he omitted mention of him explicitly because mention of his people suffices, as he is more entitled to it than they are. Or it is meant that ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ refers to Pharaoh himself.

The first is preferable, because they were all punished in this world by drowning, and they will be punished in the Hereafter by the Fire.

Then He, glorified is He, explained what had been stated in general about the evil punishment, saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾. The ﴿al-nār﴾ (the Fire) is nominative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿sū' al-ʿadhāb﴾ (the evil punishment). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ (they are exposed). The first is preferable, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. On the last two readings, the sentence is a new sentence (mustaʾnafa) answering an implied question.

It was also read in the accusative (al-nār), on the assumption of a verb implied by ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ in meaning, i.e., "they lead the Fire, they are exposed to it," or on the basis of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive (al-nāri) as a substitution for ﴿al-ʿadhāb﴾.

The majority held that this exposure is in the barzakh (the intermediate state), and it has been said: it is in the Hereafter.

Al-Farra' said: there is in the verse an inversion (taqdīm and taʾkhīr), i.e., "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment, the Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening." But there is no need for this strained reading, for His saying ﴿And on the day the Hour arises: admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ clearly indicates that this exposure is in the barzakh. His saying ﴿admit﴾ is by implied speech: it is said to the angels, "Admit the people of Pharaoh," and ﴿the most severe punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Fire.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Ḥafṣ read ﴿adkhilū﴾ with an open hamzah and a kasrah on the kha', and this is on the assumption of implied speech as mentioned. The rest read ﴿udkhulū﴾ with a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamzah) from ﴿dakhala yadkhulu﴾ as an imperative to the people of Pharaoh to enter, with the vocative particle implied: i.e., "Enter, O people of Pharaoh, the most severe punishment."

﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed by an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember).

The meaning: Remember for your people the time when they dispute with one another in the Fire. Then He, glorified is He, explained this dispute, saying: ﴿So the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, regarding submission to the prophets and following them, and they are the leaders of disbelief. ﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾: ﴿tabaʿan﴾ (followers) is the plural of ﴿tābiʿ﴾, like ﴿khadam﴾ and ﴿khādim﴾ (servants), or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of the active participle, i.e., "following," or there is an omitted genitive, i.e., "possessors of following." The Basrans said: ﴿tabaʿ﴾ can be singular and can be plural. The Kufans said it is a plural with no singular. ﴿So will you bear for us a portion of the Fire?﴾: that is, will you ward off from us a portion of it or carry it with us? The accusative of ﴿naṣīban﴾ (a portion) is by an implied verb indicated by ﴿mughnūna﴾ (you bear/avert), i.e., "will you ward off from us a portion, or prevent (it)," on the basis of implying the meaning of ﴿ḥāmilīn﴾ (carrying), i.e., "will you be carrying with us a portion?", or on the basis of it being a verbal noun.

﴿Those who were arrogant said: we are all in it﴾: this sentence is a new sentence answering an implied question, and the meaning is: we and you together are in Hell, so how can we avail you?

The majority read ﴿kullun﴾ (all) in the nominative, as the subject, with ﴿fīhā﴾ (in it) as its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed), as al-Akhfash said. Ibn al-Sumayfa' and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read ﴿kullan﴾ in the accusative. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it is for emphasis of the subject of ﴿inna﴾, with the meaning of ﴿kullunā﴾ (all of us), and its tanwin (nunation) is a substitute for the omitted genitive. It has also been said: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and Ibn Mālik preferred this.

﴿Indeed God has judged between the servants﴾: that is, He decided between them, that a group is in Paradise and a group is in the blazing Fire.

﴿And those who are in the Fire will say﴾, from the disbelieving nations, their arrogant and their weak, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾: ﴿khazana﴾ is the plural of ﴿khāzin﴾ (keeper), who is the one in charge of punishing the people of the Fire. ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment﴾: ﴿yawman﴾ (a day) is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿yukhaffif﴾ (lighten), and the object of ﴿yukhaffif﴾ is omitted: i.e., lighten for us some of the punishment to the extent of a day, or within a day.

The clause ﴿Did not your messengers used to come to you with clear proofs?﴾ is a new sentence answering an implied question, and the interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. ﴿They said: Yes﴾: that is, they came to us with them, but we denied them and did not believe in them, nor in what they brought of clear arguments. When they acknowledged this, the angels, who are the keepers of Hell, said to them, ﴿So call (upon Him)﴾: that is, if the matter is as such, then you call, for we do not call upon (Him) for one who disbelieved in God and denied His messengers after their coming with clear proofs.

Then they informed them that their call would not benefit anything, so they said: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾: that is, in loss, void, ruin, and destruction.

The clause ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ is a new sentence from His side, glorified is He: that is, We will make them the victors over their enemies and the subduers of them. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is in the accusative position, coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿rusulanā﴾ (Our messengers), i.e., "We will surely help Our messengers, and We will help those who believe along with them in the life of this world," by what God has accustomed them of retribution against them through killing, plundering, capturing, and subjugation, ﴿and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ (the witnesses) are the angels and the prophets.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ are the angels, who bear witness for the prophets that they conveyed (the message), and against the nations that they denied.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ is the plural of ﴿shāhid﴾ (witness), like ﴿ṣāḥib﴾ and ﴿aṣḥāb﴾ (companion, companions). Al-Nahhas said: the pattern fāʿil is not (normally) pluralized to afʿāl, and it is not analogized upon; rather, whatever comes of it heard (from the Arabs) is recited as it is heard. So it is, on this view, the plural of ﴿shahīd﴾, like ﴿sharīf﴾ and ﴿ashrāf﴾. The meaning of their being helped on the day when the witnesses stand is that God will recompense them for their deeds, so He admits them to Paradise and honors them with His honors, and He recompenses the disbelievers for their deeds, so He curses them and admits them to the Fire.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿On the day when the excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them, and for them is the curse﴾: that is, distance from mercy, and for them is the evil abode, that is, the Fire. ﴿The day﴾ (yawma) is a substitute for ﴿yawma yaqūmu al-ashhād﴾ (the day the witnesses stand). Their excuse did not benefit them because it was a false excuse, a rejected pretext, and a deviant doubt.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿tanfaʿu﴾ (will benefit) with the feminine (taʾ fawqiyya, upper ta'), and Nafi' and the Kufans read it with the masculine (yāʾ taḥtiyya, lower yā'). Both are permissible in the language.

Al-Bukhari recorded in his Tarikh, and Ibn al-Mundhir (recorded) from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾, that he said: they are the shedders of blood unjustly.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others recorded from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and the evening: if he is among the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is among the people of the Fire, then (it is shown) from the people of the Fire. It is said to him: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Ibn Mardawayh added: "Then he recited, ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No doer of good, whether a Muslim or a disbeliever, does good except that God rewards him." We said: "O Messenger of God, what is the reward of the disbeliever?" He said: "Wealth, children, health, and the like of that." We said: "And what is his reward in the Hereafter?" He said: "A punishment less than the (full) punishment." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited, ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever defends the honor of his brother, God will ward the Fire of Hell from his face on the Day of Resurrection." Then he recited, ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾. Ibn Mardawayh recorded a similar (report) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

This man of faith repeated his call to them to (follow) God and openly declared his faith. He did not take the earlier approaches, in which he had given them the impression that he was one of them. He stood up to admonish them only out of dislike that some of what Moses had threatened them with should befall them, as a man who loves his people would warn them against falling into what he fears for them. So he said: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter) with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ That is: tell me about your situation. I call you to salvation from the Fire and to entering Paradise through faith in God and obedience to His messengers, while you call me to the Fire by what you want from me of shirk (associating others with God).

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿ma li﴾ (what is with me) is "what is (the matter) with you that I call you," as you say, "What is with me that I see you sad?", meaning "What is with you?"

Then he explained the two calls, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾. So the phrase ﴿tad'unani﴾ (you call me) is either a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿tad'unani﴾ or an explanation of it. ﴿Of which I have no knowledge﴾ means: I have no knowledge that it is a partner of God. ﴿And I call you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving﴾: that is, to the Almighty in His retribution against those who disbelieve, and the Oft-Forgiving toward the sin of those who believe in Him.

The ﴿lā﴾ that precedes it is for negating what they claimed and refuting what they asserted. The subject of this verb is His saying: ﴿that what you call me to has no call (no efficacy) in this world or in the Hereafter﴾, that is: it is established and necessary that the call to it is void.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it has no answered call that benefits. It has also been said: it has no call that would entitle it to divinity in this world or in the Hereafter.

Al-Kalbi said: it has no intercession. ﴿And that our return is to God﴾: that is, our place of return and our destination is to Him, first through death and then through resurrection, and He will repay each person with what he deserves of good and evil. ﴿And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who greatly increase their disobedience to God. Qatadah and Ibn Sirin said: it means the polytheists. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: they are the foolish, those who shed blood unjustly. Ikrimah said: the tyrants and the arrogant. It has also been said: they are those who transgress the limits of God. The ﴿anna﴾ (that) in both places is coordinated (ʿatf) with the ﴿anna﴾ in His saying ﴿that what you call me to﴾, and the meaning is: and it is true that our return is to God, and it is true that the transgressors, etc.

﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾: when the punishment descends upon you, and you will know that I have indeed exerted myself in advising and admonishing you. In this vagueness there is a threat and intimidation that is not hidden. ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾: that is, I rely upon Him and surrender my affair to Him.

It has been said: he said this when they intended to harm him. Muqatil said: this believing man fled to the mountain and they could not reach him. It has also been said: the speaker is Moses, but the first (view) is preferable.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ (p-1303): that is, God protected him from the evil plot and the harm they intended for him. Qatadah said: God delivered him along with the Children of Israel.

﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh the terrible punishment﴾: that is, it encompassed them and descended upon them, the evil punishment.

Al-Kisa'i said: one says ﴿ḥaqa yaḥīqu ḥayqan wa-ḥuyūqan﴾ (it befell, it encompassed) when it descends and clings. Al-Kalbi said: they drowned in the sea and entered the Fire. By ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ is meant Pharaoh and his people; he omitted mention of him explicitly because mention of his people suffices, as he is more entitled to it than they are. Or it is meant that ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ refers to Pharaoh himself.

The first is preferable, because they were all punished in this world by drowning, and they will be punished in the Hereafter by the Fire.

Then He, glorified is He, explained what had been stated in general about the evil punishment, saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾. The ﴿al-nār﴾ (the Fire) is nominative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿sū' al-ʿadhāb﴾ (the evil punishment). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ (they are exposed). The first is preferable, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. On the last two readings, the sentence is a new sentence (mustaʾnafa) answering an implied question.

It was also read in the accusative (al-nār), on the assumption of a verb implied by ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ in meaning, i.e., "they lead the Fire, they are exposed to it," or on the basis of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive (al-nāri) as a substitution for ﴿al-ʿadhāb﴾.

The majority held that this exposure is in the barzakh (the intermediate state), and it has been said: it is in the Hereafter.

His saying ﴿admit﴾ is by implied speech: it is said to the angels, "Admit the people of Pharaoh," and ﴿the most severe punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Fire.

The rest read ﴿udkhulū﴾ with a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamzah) from ﴿dakhala yadkhulu﴾ as an imperative to the people of Pharaoh to enter, with the vocative particle implied: i.e., "Enter, O people of Pharaoh, the most severe punishment."

﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed by an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember).

The meaning: Remember for your people the time when they dispute with one another in the Fire. Then He, glorified is He, explained this dispute, saying: ﴿So the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, regarding submission to the prophets and following them, and they are the leaders of disbelief. ﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾: ﴿tabaʿan﴾ (followers) is the plural of ﴿tābiʿ﴾, like ﴿khadam﴾ and ﴿khādim﴾ (servants), or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of the active participle, i.e., "following," or there is an omitted genitive, i.e., "possessors of following." The Basrans said: ﴿tabaʿ﴾ can be singular and can be plural. The Kufans said it is a plural with no singular. ﴿So will you bear for us a portion of the Fire?﴾: that is, will you ward off from us a portion of it or carry it with us? It has also been said: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and Ibn Mālik preferred this.

﴿Indeed God has judged between the servants﴾: that is, He decided between them, that a group is in Paradise and a group is in the blazing Fire.

﴿And those who are in the Fire will say﴾, from the disbelieving nations, their arrogant and their weak, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾: ﴿khazana﴾ is the plural of ﴿khāzin﴾ (keeper), who is the one in charge of punishing the people of the Fire. ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment﴾: ﴿yawman﴾ (a day) is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿yukhaffif﴾ (lighten), and the object of ﴿yukhaffif﴾ is omitted: i.e., lighten for us some of the punishment to the extent of a day, or within a day.

When they acknowledged this, the angels, who are the keepers of Hell, said to them, ﴿So call (upon Him)﴾: that is, if the matter is as such, then you call, for we do not call upon (Him) for one who disbelieved in God and denied His messengers after their coming with clear proofs.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it is for emphasis of the subject of ﴿inna﴾, with the meaning of ﴿kullunā﴾ (all of us), and its tanwin (nunation) is a substitute for the omitted genitive. It has also been said: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and Ibn Mālik preferred this.

﴿Indeed God has judged between the servants﴾: that is, He decided between them, that a group is in Paradise and a group is in the blazing Fire.

﴿And those who are in the Fire will say﴾, from the disbelieving nations, their arrogant and their weak, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾: ﴿khazana﴾ is the plural of ﴿khāzin﴾ (keeper), who is the one in charge of punishing the people of the Fire. ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment﴾: ﴿yawman﴾ (a day) is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿yukhaffif﴾ (lighten), and the object of ﴿yukhaffif﴾ is omitted: i.e., lighten for us some of the punishment to the extent of a day, or within a day.

The clause ﴿Did not your messengers used to come to you with clear proofs?﴾ is a new sentence answering an implied question, and the interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. ﴿They said: Yes﴾: that is, they came to us with them, but we denied them and did not believe in them, nor in what they brought of clear arguments. When they acknowledged this, the angels, who are the keepers of Hell, said to them, ﴿So call (upon Him)﴾: that is, if the matter is as such, then you call, for we do not call upon (Him) for one who disbelieved in God and denied His messengers after their coming with clear proofs.

Then they informed them that their call would not benefit anything, so they said: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾: that is, in loss, void, ruin, and destruction.

The clause ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ is a new sentence from His side, glorified is He: that is, We will make them the victors over their enemies and the subduers of them. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is in the accusative position, coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿rusulanā﴾ (Our messengers), i.e., "We will surely help Our messengers, and We will help those who believe along with them in the life of this world," by what God has accustomed them of retribution against them through killing, plundering, capturing, and subjugation, ﴿and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ (the witnesses) are the angels and the prophets.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ are the angels, who bear witness for the prophets that they conveyed (the message), and against the nations that they denied.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ is the plural of ﴿shāhid﴾ (witness), like ﴿ṣāḥib﴾ and ﴿aṣḥāb﴾ (companion, companions). Al-Nahhas said: the pattern fāʿil is not (normally) pluralized to afʿāl, and it is not analogized upon; rather, whatever comes of it heard (from the Arabs) is recited as it is heard. So it is, on this view, the plural of ﴿shahīd﴾, like ﴿sharīf﴾ and ﴿ashrāf﴾. The meaning of their being helped on the day when the witnesses stand is that God will recompense them for their deeds, so He admits them to Paradise and honors them with His honors, and He recompenses the disbelievers for their deeds, so He curses them and admits them to the Fire.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿On the day when the excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them, and for them is the curse﴾: that is, distance from mercy, and for them is the evil abode, that is, the Fire. ﴿The day﴾ (yawma) is a substitute for ﴿yawma yaqūmu al-ashhād﴾ (the day the witnesses stand). Their excuse did not benefit them because it was a false excuse, a rejected pretext, and a deviant doubt.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿tanfaʿu﴾ (will benefit) with the feminine (taʾ fawqiyya, upper ta'), and Nafi' and the Kufans read it with the masculine (yāʾ taḥtiyya, lower yā'). Both are permissible in the language.

Al-Bukhari recorded in his Tarikh, and Ibn al-Mundhir (recorded) from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾, that he said: they are the shedders of blood unjustly.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others recorded from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and the evening: if he is among the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is among the people of the Fire, then (it is shown) from the people of the Fire. It is said to him: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Ibn Mardawayh added: "Then he recited, ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No doer of good, whether a Muslim or a disbeliever, does good except that God rewards him." We said: "O Messenger of God, what is the reward of the disbeliever?" He said: "Wealth, children, health, and the like of that." We said: "And what is his reward in the Hereafter?" He said: "A punishment less than the (full) punishment." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited, ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever defends the honor of his brother, God will ward the Fire of Hell from his face on the Day of Resurrection." Then he recited, ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾. Ibn Mardawayh recorded a similar (report) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

This man of faith repeated his call to them to (follow) God and openly declared his faith. He did not take the earlier approaches, in which he had given them the impression that he was one of them. He stood up to admonish them only out of dislike that some of what Moses had threatened them with should befall them, as a man who loves his people would warn them against falling into what he fears for them. So he said: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter) with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ That is: tell me about your situation. I call you to salvation from the Fire and to entering Paradise through faith in God and obedience to His messengers, while you call me to the Fire by what you want from me of shirk (associating others with God).

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿ma li﴾ (what is with me) is "what is (the matter) with you that I call you," as you say, "What is with me that I see you sad?", meaning "What is with you?"

Then he explained the two calls, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾. So the phrase ﴿tad'unani﴾ (you call me) is either a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿tad'unani﴾ or an explanation of it. ﴿Of which I have no knowledge﴾ means: I have no knowledge that it is a partner of God. ﴿And I call you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving﴾: that is, to the Almighty in His retribution against those who disbelieve, and the Oft-Forgiving toward the sin of those who believe in Him.

Al-Kalbi said: it has no intercession. ﴿And that our return is to God﴾: that is, our place of return and our destination is to Him, first through death and then through resurrection, and He will repay each person with what he deserves of good and evil. ﴿And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who greatly increase their disobedience to God. Qatadah and Ibn Sirin said: it means the polytheists. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: they are the foolish, those who shed blood unjustly. Ikrimah said: the tyrants and the arrogant. It has also been said: they are those who transgress the limits of God. The ﴿anna﴾ (that) in both places is coordinated (ʿatf) with the ﴿anna﴾ in His saying ﴿that what you call me to﴾, and the meaning is: and it is true that our return is to God, and it is true that the transgressors, etc.

﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾: when the punishment descends upon you, and you will know that I have indeed exerted myself in advising and admonishing you. In this vagueness there is a threat and intimidation that is not hidden. ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾: that is, I rely upon Him and surrender my affair to Him.

It has been said: he said this when they intended to harm him. Muqatil said: this believing man fled to the mountain and they could not reach him. It has also been said: the speaker is Moses, but the first (view) is preferable.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ (p-1303): that is, God protected him from the evil plot and the harm they intended for him. Qatadah said: God delivered him along with the Children of Israel.

﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh the terrible punishment﴾: that is, it encompassed them and descended upon them, the evil punishment.

Al-Kisa'i said: one says ﴿ḥaqa yaḥīqu ḥayqan wa-ḥuyūqan﴾ (it befell, it encompassed) when it descends and clings. Al-Kalbi said: they drowned in the sea and entered the Fire. Or it is meant that ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ refers to Pharaoh himself.

The first is preferable, because they were all punished in this world by drowning, and they will be punished in the Hereafter by the Fire.

On the last two readings, the sentence is a new sentence (mustaʾnafa) answering an implied question.

The majority held that this exposure is in the barzakh (the intermediate state), and it has been said: it is in the Hereafter.

﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed by an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember).

The meaning: Remember for your people the time when they dispute with one another in the Fire. Then He, glorified is He, explained this dispute, saying: ﴿So the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, regarding submission to the prophets and following them, and they are the leaders of disbelief. ﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾: ﴿tabaʿan﴾ (followers) is the plural of ﴿tābiʿ﴾, like ﴿khadam﴾ and ﴿khādim﴾ (servants), or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of the active participle, i.e., "following," or there is an omitted genitive, i.e., "possessors of following." The Basrans said: ﴿tabaʿ﴾ can be singular and can be plural. The Kufans said it is a plural with no singular. ﴿So will you bear for us a portion of the Fire?﴾: that is, will you ward off from us a portion of it or carry it with us? The accusative of ﴿naṣīban﴾ (a portion) is by an implied verb indicated by ﴿mughnūna﴾ (you bear/avert), i.e., "will you ward off from us a portion, or prevent (it)," on the basis of implying the meaning of ﴿ḥāmilīn﴾ (carrying), i.e., "will you be carrying with us a portion?", or on the basis of it being a verbal noun.

﴿And when they argue with one another in the Fire﴾: the adverbial clause (al-ẓarf) is in the accusative, governed by an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember).

The meaning: Remember for your people the time when they dispute with one another in the Fire. Then He, glorified is He, explained this dispute, saying: ﴿So the weak will say to those who were arrogant﴾, regarding submission to the prophets and following them, and they are the leaders of disbelief. ﴿Indeed, we were following you﴾: ﴿tabaʿan﴾ (followers) is the plural of ﴿tābiʿ﴾, like ﴿khadam﴾ and ﴿khādim﴾ (servants), or it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning in the position of the active participle, i.e., "following," or there is an omitted genitive, i.e., "possessors of following." The Basrans said: ﴿tabaʿ﴾ can be singular and can be plural. The Kufans said it is a plural with no singular. ﴿So will you bear for us a portion of the Fire?﴾: that is, will you ward off from us a portion of it or carry it with us? The accusative of ﴿naṣīban﴾ (a portion) is by an implied verb indicated by ﴿mughnūna﴾ (you bear/avert), i.e., "will you ward off from us a portion, or prevent (it)," on the basis of implying the meaning of ﴿ḥāmilīn﴾ (carrying), i.e., "will you be carrying with us a portion?", or on the basis of it being a verbal noun.

﴿Those who were arrogant said: we are all in it﴾: this sentence is a new sentence answering an implied question, and the meaning is: we and you together are in Hell, so how can we avail you?

The majority read ﴿kullun﴾ (all) in the nominative, as the subject, with ﴿fīhā﴾ (in it) as its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed), as al-Akhfash said. Ibn al-Sumayfa' and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read ﴿kullan﴾ in the accusative. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it is for emphasis of the subject of ﴿inna﴾, with the meaning of ﴿kullunā﴾ (all of us), and its tanwin (nunation) is a substitute for the omitted genitive. It has also been said: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl), and Ibn Mālik preferred this.

﴿Indeed God has judged between the servants﴾: that is, He decided between them, that a group is in Paradise and a group is in the blazing Fire.

﴿And those who are in the Fire will say﴾, from the disbelieving nations, their arrogant and their weak, ﴿to the keepers of Hell﴾: ﴿khazana﴾ is the plural of ﴿khāzin﴾ (keeper), who is the one in charge of punishing the people of the Fire. ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us one day of the punishment﴾: ﴿yawman﴾ (a day) is an adverbial of time governed by ﴿yukhaffif﴾ (lighten), and the object of ﴿yukhaffif﴾ is omitted: i.e., lighten for us some of the punishment to the extent of a day, or within a day.

The clause ﴿Did not your messengers used to come to you with clear proofs?﴾ is a new sentence answering an implied question, and the interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. ﴿They said: Yes﴾: that is, they came to us with them, but we denied them and did not believe in them, nor in what they brought of clear arguments. When they acknowledged this, the angels, who are the keepers of Hell, said to them, ﴿So call (upon Him)﴾: that is, if the matter is as such, then you call, for we do not call upon (Him) for one who disbelieved in God and denied His messengers after their coming with clear proofs.

Then they informed them that their call would not benefit anything, so they said: ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error﴾: that is, in loss, void, ruin, and destruction.

The clause ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ is a new sentence from His side, glorified is He: that is, We will make them the victors over their enemies and the subduers of them. The relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl) is in the accusative position, coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿rusulanā﴾ (Our messengers), i.e., "We will surely help Our messengers, and We will help those who believe along with them in the life of this world," by what God has accustomed them of retribution against them through killing, plundering, capturing, and subjugation, ﴿and on the day when the witnesses stand﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ (the witnesses) are the angels and the prophets.

Mujahid and al-Suddi said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ are the angels, who bear witness for the prophets that they conveyed (the message), and against the nations that they denied.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ is the plural of ﴿shāhid﴾ (witness), like ﴿ṣāḥib﴾ and ﴿aṣḥāb﴾ (companion, companions). Al-Nahhas said: the pattern fāʿil is not (normally) pluralized to afʿāl, and it is not analogized upon; rather, whatever comes of it heard (from the Arabs) is recited as it is heard. So it is, on this view, the plural of ﴿shahīd﴾, like ﴿sharīf﴾ and ﴿ashrāf﴾. The meaning of their being helped on the day when the witnesses stand is that God will recompense them for their deeds, so He admits them to Paradise and honors them with His honors, and He recompenses the disbelievers for their deeds, so He curses them and admits them to the Fire.

This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿On the day when the excuses of the wrongdoers will not benefit them, and for them is the curse﴾: that is, distance from mercy, and for them is the evil abode, that is, the Fire. ﴿The day﴾ (yawma) is a substitute for ﴿yawma yaqūmu al-ashhād﴾ (the day the witnesses stand). Their excuse did not benefit them because it was a false excuse, a rejected pretext, and a deviant doubt.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿tanfaʿu﴾ (will benefit) with the feminine (taʾ fawqiyya, upper ta'), and Nafi' and the Kufans read it with the masculine (yāʾ taḥtiyya, lower yā'). Both are permissible in the language.

Al-Bukhari recorded in his Tarikh, and Ibn al-Mundhir (recorded) from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying ﴿and that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾, that he said: they are the shedders of blood unjustly.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others recorded from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him in the morning and the evening: if he is among the people of Paradise, then (it is shown) from the people of Paradise, and if he is among the people of the Fire, then (it is shown) from the people of the Fire. It is said to him: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Ibn Mardawayh added: "Then he recited, ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾."

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "No doer of good, whether a Muslim or a disbeliever, does good except that God rewards him." We said: "O Messenger of God, what is the reward of the disbeliever?" He said: "Wealth, children, health, and the like of that." We said: "And what is his reward in the Hereafter?" He said: "A punishment less than the (full) punishment." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited, ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾.

Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn Abi al-Dunya, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shuʿab recorded from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever defends the honor of his brother, God will ward the Fire of Hell from his face on the Day of Resurrection." Then he recited, ﴿Indeed We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾. Ibn Mardawayh recorded a similar (report) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

This man of faith repeated his call to them to (follow) God and openly declared his faith. He did not take the earlier approaches, in which he had given them the impression that he was one of them. He stood up to admonish them only out of dislike that some of what Moses had threatened them with should befall them, as a man who loves his people would warn them against falling into what he fears for them. So he said: ﴿O my people, what is (the matter) with me that I call you to salvation while you call me to the Fire?﴾ That is: tell me about your situation. I call you to salvation from the Fire and to entering Paradise through faith in God and obedience to His messengers, while you call me to the Fire by what you want from me of shirk (associating others with God).

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿ma li﴾ (what is with me) is "what is (the matter) with you that I call you," as you say, "What is with me that I see you sad?", meaning "What is with you?"

Then he explained the two calls, saying: ﴿You call me to disbelieve in God and to associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge﴾. So the phrase ﴿tad'unani﴾ (you call me) is either a substitute (badal) for the first ﴿tad'unani﴾ or an explanation of it. ﴿Of which I have no knowledge﴾ means: I have no knowledge that it is a partner of God. ﴿And I call you to the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving﴾: that is, to the Almighty in His retribution against those who disbelieve, and the Oft-Forgiving toward the sin of those who believe in Him.

The ﴿lā﴾ that precedes it is for negating what they claimed and refuting what they asserted. The subject of this verb is His saying: ﴿that what you call me to has no call (no efficacy) in this world or in the Hereafter﴾, that is: it is established and necessary that the call to it is void.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that it has no answered call that benefits. It has also been said: it has no call that would entitle it to divinity in this world or in the Hereafter.

Al-Kalbi said: it has no intercession. ﴿And that our return is to God﴾: that is, our place of return and our destination is to Him, first through death and then through resurrection, and He will repay each person with what he deserves of good and evil. ﴿And that the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾: that is, those who greatly increase their disobedience to God. Qatadah and Ibn Sirin said: it means the polytheists. Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: they are the foolish, those who shed blood unjustly. Ikrimah said: the tyrants and the arrogant. It has also been said: they are those who transgress the limits of God. The ﴿anna﴾ (that) in both places is coordinated (ʿatf) with the ﴿anna﴾ in His saying ﴿that what you call me to﴾, and the meaning is: and it is true that our return is to God, and it is true that the transgressors, etc.

﴿So you will remember what I say to you﴾: when the punishment descends upon you, and you will know that I have indeed exerted myself in advising and admonishing you. In this vagueness there is a threat and intimidation that is not hidden. ﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾: that is, I rely upon Him and surrender my affair to Him.

It has been said: he said this when they intended to harm him. Muqatil said: this believing man fled to the mountain and they could not reach him. It has also been said: the speaker is Moses, but the first (view) is preferable.

﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted﴾ (p-1303): that is, God protected him from the evil plot and the harm they intended for him. Qatadah said: God delivered him along with the Children of Israel.

﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh the terrible punishment﴾: that is, it encompassed them and descended upon them, the evil punishment.

Al-Kisa'i said: one says ﴿ḥaqa yaḥīqu ḥayqan wa-ḥuyūqan﴾ (it befell, it encompassed) when it descends and clings. Al-Kalbi said: they drowned in the sea and entered the Fire. By ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ is meant Pharaoh and his people; he omitted mention of him explicitly because mention of his people suffices, as he is more entitled to it than they are. Or it is meant that ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾ refers to Pharaoh himself.

The first is preferable, because they were all punished in this world by drowning, and they will be punished in the Hereafter by the Fire.

Then He, glorified is He, explained what had been stated in general about the evil punishment, saying: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾. The ﴿al-nār﴾ (the Fire) is nominative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿sū' al-ʿadhāb﴾ (the evil punishment). It has also been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, or it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ (they are exposed). The first is preferable, and al-Zajjaj preferred it. On the last two readings, the sentence is a new sentence (mustaʾnafa) answering an implied question.

It was also read in the accusative (al-nār), on the assumption of a verb implied by ﴿yu'raḍūna﴾ in meaning, i.e., "they lead the Fire, they are exposed to it," or on the basis of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). Al-Farra' permitted the genitive (al-nāri) as a substitution for ﴿al-ʿadhāb﴾.

The majority held that this exposure is in the barzakh (the intermediate state), and it has been said: it is in the Hereafter.

Al-Farra' said: there is in the verse an inversion (taqdīm and taʾkhīr), i.e., "Admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment, the Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening." But there is no need for this strained reading, for His saying ﴿And on the day the Hour arises: admit the people of Pharaoh to the most severe punishment﴾ clearly indicates that this exposure is in the barzakh. His saying ﴿admit﴾ is by implied speech: it is said to the angels, "Admit the people of Pharaoh," and ﴿the most severe punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Fire.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: ﴿al-ashhād﴾ (the witnesses) are the angels and the prophets.

It has been said: the meaning of ﴿ma li﴾ (what is with me) is "what is (the matter) with you that I call you," as you say, "What is with me that I see you sad?", meaning "What is with you?"
